Yes. I crawled the relevant GitHub branches far enough that there’s a pretty clear architecture emerging, and I also checked your actual `oldmangrizzz/gods-eye-view` fork rather than treating “God’s Eye View” as a generic concept.

The big conclusion is: **I would not build this as a Quest-specific application and later try to port it. I’d make OpenXR the hardware boundary from day one, with Godot as the native spatial runtime.** Quest 3 then becomes the first hardware target rather than the architecture.

Your reference images read to me as two related interaction modes: a persistent spatial cockpit surrounding the operator, and a central object/system that can be pulled apart into semantically meaningful pieces, manipulated, interrogated, and reassembled. That is completely achievable with what is on GitHub now.

### The strongest stack I found

| Layer | GitHub project | My assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Native XR runtime | `godotengine/godot` | **Best primary foundation** |
| Quest/OpenXR vendor features | `GodotVR/godot_openxr_vendors` | **Critical piece** |
| Physics | Godot/Jolt physics | **Use this first** |
| Exploded-view reference | `xeokit/xeokit-sdk` | **Best implementation reference, not necessarily runtime** |
| Quest-native MR reference | `oculus-samples/Unity-MRUtilityKitSample` | **Excellent reference implementation** |
| Depth/real-world occlusion | `oculus-samples/Unity-DepthAPI` | **Reference for desired behavior** |
| Quest camera access | `oculus-samples/Unity-PassthroughCameraApiSamples` | **Useful perception reference** |
| Lightweight alternate XR runtime | `StereoKit/StereoKit` | **Very attractive Plan B/prototyper** |
| Web/XR fallback | `playcanvas/engine` | **Best web-first option I found** |
| XR Gaussian splats | `mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D` | **Very relevant bridge** |
| 3DGS training/reconstruction | `nerfstudio-project/gsplat`, `nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio` | **Server/workstation side** |
| Reference 3DGS | `graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting` | **Research/reference side** |

The reason **Godot jumps ahead of Unity for your particular use case** is `GodotVR/godot_openxr_vendors`. It isn't just a theoretical OpenXR compatibility shim. The current repository has working Meta-specific samples for passthrough, hand tracking, body tracking, spatial anchors and scene understanding. Its Meta Scene Manager documentation explicitly says it can obtain the scanned room mesh on Quest 3, along with semantic things such as walls, doors and tables. The sample code turns the global scene mesh into collision geometry. The repository is also actively maintained—the GitHub API shows a September 23, 2026 push—and is predominantly MIT licensed.

That gives you an extremely important chain:

**real room → Quest Scene API → semantic/global mesh → collision geometry → physics world → manipulable XR objects.**

That is already most of the substrate you need for what you're describing.

And it lines up almost absurdly well with the spatial architecture you've already written. Your Ambient Spatial Cockpit document already specifies scene reconstruction through COLMAP, Gaussian Splatting, Nerfstudio/PanSplat and point geometry. fileciteturn0file1L64-L95 It then moves through ORB-SLAM3/stella_vslam localization and COVINS-G/DOOR-SLAM shared-map consensus. fileciteturn0file1L249-L283 At the visualization end, you've already specified an asset-light procedural GPU model and direct spatial buffers rather than conventional heavyweight scene assets. fileciteturn0file1L451-L487

So I don't think you need a new architecture. **XR is essentially the missing presentation/interaction layer on top of the architecture you've already designed.**

### The exploded-view part is actually easier than it looks

`xeokit/xeokit-sdk` turned out to be a particularly good find. It is an engineering/BIM viewer, and the repo contains an explicit **exploded-model example** (`OBJ_SportsCar_ExplodeModel`) plus section-plane support. So somebody has already solved the interaction/modeling problem you're describing in a domain with thousands of individually addressable components.

I would borrow the **model**, not necessarily xeokit itself.

You want each meaningful thing represented something like:

```text
Assembly
 ├── subsystem
 │    ├── component
 │    │    ├── mesh / splat / primitive
 │    │    ├── home transform
 │    │    ├── exploded transform
 │    │    ├── physics body
 │    │    ├── constraints
 │    │    └── semantic metadata
 │    └── component
 └── subsystem
```

Then `"explode = 0.0 → 1.0"` simply interpolates every part from its assembly transform toward its exploded transform.

Where it gets interesting—and much closer to what you're envisioning—is that it needn't just be visual.

Grab the transmission out of a virtual vehicle with your hand and its rigid body wakes up. Pull one subsystem away and connecting lines/flows remain visible. Ask what the component does and the semantic node gives the AI its context. Freeze physics and view force vectors. Reassemble it and constraints snap the components back into the correct topology.

That turns “exploded view” into an **interactive semantic digital twin**, rather than an animation.

One caution with xeokit: its current README states AGPLv3 for the SDK unless you obtain their commercial licensing. So I'd study its technique and examples rather than making it a core dependency unless that licensing fits what you're doing.

### Your God's Eye View fork becomes a data plane, not the XR engine

I inspected `oldmangrizzz/gods-eye-view`. The current project is vanilla JavaScript + CesiumJS + Vite and already has the right conceptual primitives: live entities, target tracking, proximity contacts, world-space headings, trails, routes, sensor treatments, annotations and a context-aware agent.

I would **not** try to shove CesiumJS wholesale inside the Quest native application.

Instead:

```text
                     GOD'S EYE VIEW
                  global contextual state
                          │
             aircraft / traffic / terrain /
             routes / weather / infrastructure
                          │
                    Spatial Gateway
                 WGS84 → local ENU frame
                          │
            ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
            │                            │
     Godot/OpenXR World           World-model server
     Quest / PC / future XR       inference / 3DGS /
            │                     simulation
            │                            │
            └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                          │
                  Semantic World Graph
                          │
               physics + relationships
                          │
          exploded / assembled / simulation
```

That WGS84 → local metric projection boundary isn't something I'm inventing here either. Your cockpit architecture already defines the emergency/operator position as a local ENU tangent-plane origin specifically so downstream rendering can work in ordinary Cartesian coordinates. fileciteturn0file1L198-L230

That's exactly what an XR engine wants.

God's Eye View therefore supplies the **macro world**.

Quest supplies the **immediate physical world**.

SLAM/scene reconstruction supplies the **local reconstructed world**.

And the semantic graph becomes the thing that makes all three understandable as one environment.

### Now the “little self-hosted Genie 3” part

This is where I'd make one important conceptual distinction.

The PDF you uploaded titled *Building Genie* is Cosine's software-engineering Genie, not Google's Genie-family interactive-world model. Its useful architectural lesson here is the agentic loop: planning, retrieval, code writing and execution. fileciteturn0file0L127-L148 So it can inform the **agent/reasoning layer**, but it isn't itself the world-simulation technology you're looking for.

For your “small Genie 3” objective, I would **not try to make the Quest run the world model**.

Make the Quest an extraordinarily good sensor/rendering/interaction endpoint.

The self-hosted machine does:

```text
observations
     ↓
scene reconstruction / perception
     ↓
semantic state graph
     ↓
world-state model
     ↓
predicted or generated state transitions
     ↓
explicit physics validation
     ↓
scene delta
     ↓
Quest
```

That hybrid is considerably more useful than simply trying to clone a generative video model.

You would have two representations of reality simultaneously:

**Explicit state:** objects, transforms, velocity, mass, constraints, semantic relationships, location, confidence and provenance.

**Neural appearance:** Gaussian splats / reconstructed surfaces / generated visual state.

Physics governs what *can happen*.

The learned model predicts what *might happen*.

XR lets the operator walk around inside the result.

That's where `gsplat`/Nerfstudio fit very naturally. And `mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D` was a particularly interesting find because it already contains built-in WebXR VR and AR support and can mix Three.js geometry with Gaussian splats. That makes it a nice experimental bridge while the native renderer is being developed.

Your existing document actually anticipates this division: its end-to-end pipeline terminates in a GPU-consumable local spatial representation rather than insisting that the data source and renderer be one monolithic system. fileciteturn0file1L609-L642

### There are really three viable implementation paths

**Godot/OpenXR is the one I'd choose for the real system.** Native Quest APK first; Meta passthrough/Scene API/anchors/hands; physics in-process; OpenXR as the portability seam. Later the same application architecture can target other OpenXR runtimes instead of rewriting the product.

**StereoKit is the one I'd use if we wanted an absurdly fast proof of concept.** The repo explicitly supports Meta Quest, OpenXR, Android ARM64, hand input, glTF/GLB/OBJ/STL/PLY and physics. I also found actual Quest passthrough code and an Android manifest explicitly listing Quest 3. It is remarkably close to “write a few hundred lines and see if Grizz's idea feels right.” Its weakness is that I did not find the same level of Meta Scene API support that the Godot vendor stack currently exposes.

**PlayCanvas + GaussianSplats3D is the browser path.** PlayCanvas now has WebXR, WebGPU/WebGL, Gaussian splatting and physics in the same engine. GaussianSplats3D separately provides explicit WebXR VR/AR modes. This would get something spectacular running through Quest Browser quickly, and it is inherently portable. But I'd regard it as a demonstrator or thin client, not the final substrate, because native Meta scene/depth/camera capabilities matter too much for the system you're describing.

Unity/MRUK is technically excellent and Meta's official sample repositories are valuable. In fact, the current MRUK sample demonstrates scene visualization, room-aware spawning, nav meshes and global meshes, while Meta's Depth API samples demonstrate real-world occlusion on Quest 3-class hardware. Their passthrough-camera samples specifically target Quest 3/3S and expose actual camera frames. I would use all three as **behavioral specifications and test cases** while keeping your core architecture OpenXR/open-source.

### What I'd build first

Not the globe. Not the AI. Not 3DGS.

I'd make a **Quest 3 “exploded room” vertical slice**:

The native Apple app should consume a distilled state feed from this runtime instead of embedding the complete browser renderer as its spatial core.')
add_table(doc,['Bridge contract','Direction','Content'],[
('WorldStateSnapshot','GEV -> Apple','camera/global anchor, active map context, selected target, visible entity summaries, timebase'),
('EntityDelta','GEV -> Apple','id, source, WGS84 location, velocity/heading, classification, confidence, timestamp'),
('LocalAnchor','Apple -> GEV','chosen WGS84 origin and AR-local pose used to establish ENU mapping'),
('Selection / annotation','Bidirectional','selected entity, labels, user markups, scene commands'),
('Splat registration state','Apple/Mac -> GEV','capture id, local anchor, registration transform, confidence, version'),
], widths=[1.55,1.25,4.4])
p=doc.add_paragraph('The Apple bridge should use `URLSessionWebSocketTask` for the first implementation. The data schema should be binary-friendly from the start (for example, MessagePack/CBOR/FlatBuffers later), but JSON is acceptable for the tracer-bullet milestone.')

h=doc.add_heading('5.1 Coordinate Contract', level=2); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('The global-to-local contract should continue the existing GMRI WGS84-to-ENU approach. A selected operational origin defines the tangent frame. God’s Eye View entities arrive in WGS84; the gateway converts them to local ENU meters; the Apple client maps that metric frame into the ARKit world transform. This prevents Cesium-scale floating-point and geodetic concerns from leaking into local physics and interaction.')
add_code_block(doc,
'''Global WGS84 entity\n      |\n      v\nECEF / ENU transform around chosen anchor\n      |     (meters, local tangent frame)\n      v\nT_enu_to_arworld  ----> RealityKit Entity.transform\n      |\n      +----> physics / interaction / splat registration use the same local metric frame''')

# 6 semantic scene graph
h=doc.add_heading('6. Semantic Scene Graph and Exploded-View Model', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('The exploded-view capability should be a property of the semantic scene graph, not a one-off animation. Each addressable assembly part has a persistent identity, hierarchy, home transform, exploded transform, interaction state, physical proxy, metadata, and provenance. This makes the same structure usable for training, simulation, maintenance visualization, anatomy, machinery, buildings, or any other decomposable system.')
add_code_block(doc,
'''AssemblyNode\n  id / semanticType / provenance\n  parent / children[]\n  homeTransform\n  explodeVector or explodeTransform\n  renderRepresentation\n    - mesh / primitive / splat region reference\n  physicsRepresentation\n    - collider / mass / constraints / mode\n  telemetryBindings[]\n  annotations[]\n  confidence / lifecycle state''')

add_table(doc,['Exploded-view function','Implementation'],[
('Explode / reassemble','Interpolate each node between home and exploded transforms; preserve hierarchy.'),
('Grab / inspect','InputTarget + collision shape; convert selected part to kinematic/dynamic as appropriate.'),
('Physics release','Switch from authored transform control to RealityKit dynamic body; constraints remain explicit.'),
('Cross-section / isolate','Visibility/material state at semantic-node level; optional clipping shader.'),
('Flow overlays','Procedural line/particle entities bound to graph edges (power, fluid, data, force, etc.).'),
('AI interrogation','Prompt context is retrieved from the selected node, parent assembly, telemetry, and provenance.'),
], widths=[1.8,5.4])

add_callout(doc,'Design rule','Do not use Gaussian splats as the authoritative exploded-view hierarchy. Splats are excellent for appearance; they are poor as a primary semantic/physics structure. Keep exploded components as explicit scene nodes and let splats decorate, contextualize, or reconstruct the surrounding environment.','F2EEF8')

# 7 splat architecture
h=doc.add_heading('7. Gaussian Splat Architecture', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('Apple hardware now has several viable open-source Metal 3DGS paths. For the first implementation, `scier/MetalSplatter` is the most pragmatic renderer because it is a Swift/Metal library explicitly supporting iOS, iPad, macOS, and visionOS, accepts PLY/SPZ/.splat, and is MIT licensed. It is intentionally under-documented, so GMRI should fork and wrap it behind a narrow internal interface rather than allowing its API to spread through the application.')
add_table(doc,['Repository','Best use in this architecture','Readiness','License / caveat'],[
('scier/MetalSplatter','Initial Apple-native splat renderer','Good prototype / proven integration base','MIT; documentation sparse'),
('studiomeije/GSKit','Reference for RealityKit-native splat ownership via LowLevelMesh + CustomMaterial','Experimental; macOS 26 only today','MIT; excellent architectural reference'),
('LuckyIYI/gsm-renderer','Advanced renderer experiments: SH 0-3, multiple sorting paths, optional depth texture','WIP / not production-ready','Verify license before adoption; use as reference unless stabilized'),
('PoSTMEDIA-AI/splatx-metal','Self-hosted Apple Silicon training, alignment, SPZ distribution, optional on-device training','Pre-1.0 but unusually strong verification/provenance story','Apache-2.0; Apple Silicon only'),
('frs0n/msplat-ios','Evidence that Metal training can be pushed onto iPhone-class hardware','Research / specialized','Use only if on-device training becomes a requirement'),
], widths=[1.45,2.55,1.45,2.05])

h=doc.add_heading('7.1 Recommended Render Interface', level=2); keep_with_next(h)
add_code_block(doc,
'''protocol SplatLayerRenderer {\n    func load(scene: SplatSceneDescriptor) async throws -> SplatHandle\n    func setWorldTransform(_ transform: simd_float4x4, for handle: SplatHandle)\n    func setOpacity(_ alpha: Float, for handle: SplatHandle)\n    func setVisibility(_ visible: Bool, for handle: SplatHandle)\n    func updateCamera(_ camera: SpatialCameraState)\n    func render(into target: SpatialRenderTarget) throws\n    func unload(_ handle: SplatHandle)\n}''')
p=doc.add_paragraph('This isolates the application from sorting strategy, file format, and Metal implementation. It also leaves room to replace MetalSplatter with a RealityKit-native LowLevelMesh path later without rewriting the semantic world model.')

# bridge crossing
h=doc.add_heading('8. Bridge Crossing: Local Environment Splat Overlay', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('The unique local-environment overlay should be implemented as an explicit registration state machine. The critical problem is not loading another splat file; it is proving that the splat coordinate frame is correctly registered to the live ARKit world and remains stable enough to cross from “preview” into “world-locked overlay.”')
add_code_block(doc,
'''CAPTURED -> RECONSTRUCTED -> CANDIDATE_REGISTERED -> VERIFIED -> BRIDGED -> DEGRADED\n\nCAPTURED:            frames + ARKit poses + intrinsics recorded\nRECONSTRUCTED:       PLY/SPZ and camera trajectory produced\nCANDIDATE_REGISTERED: similarity transform estimated\nVERIFIED:            residuals and scale remain inside thresholds\nBRIDGED:             splat overlay fades in / becomes world-stable\nDEGRADED:            tracking or registration confidence falls; overlay fades or freezes''')

h=doc.add_heading('8.1 Registration Method', level=2); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('The preferred path is pose-driven registration because the same device that captures the environment already knows its ARKit camera poses. Store timestamped AR camera transforms and intrinsics with every captured frame. During reconstruction, retain the corresponding reconstructed camera trajectory. Estimate a similarity transform (scale + rotation + translation) between the reconstructed camera centers and the ARKit trajectory. Use point-cloud/mesh ICP only as a secondary refinement or recovery mechanism.')
add_bullets(doc,[
'Primary alignment: paired camera poses -> robust Sim(3) estimate (RANSAC/Umeyama-family fit).',
'Secondary refinement: ARKit scene mesh / point samples against Gaussian means or a derived proxy point cloud.',
'Validation: translation residual, angular residual, scale drift, inlier fraction, and temporal stability.',
'Activation: cross-fade splat opacity only after registration is stable for a bounded observation window.',
'Recovery: if AR tracking relocalizes or the world map changes, re-evaluate transform confidence before continuing.'
])

h=doc.add_heading('8.2 Occlusion and Physics Rule', level=2); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('The splat layer should be visual-only in the first implementation. Real-world occlusion and collision should come from ARKit scene reconstruction or generated proxy geometry. This is both simpler and more physically honest: a Gaussian field is a rendering representation, not a collision manifold. When the splat and mesh disagree, interaction should follow the explicit mesh/proxy state and the discrepancy should be measurable rather than hidden.')

h=doc.add_heading('8.3 Difficulty of Adding Additional Splat Layers', level=2); keep_with_next(h)
add_table(doc,['Capability','Difficulty','Main risk','Recommendation'],[
('Load one additional static splat','Moderate','Memory, load latency, sort cost','Straightforward behind a renderer abstraction; prefer SPZ for transfer/storage.'),
('Multiple registered splats in one local frame','Moderate-High','Cross-layer depth ordering and total Gaussian count','Partition by region; per-layer culling/LOD; do not globally sort everything unless necessary.'),
('Bridge Crossing registration','High but tractable','Coordinate alignment and relocalization correctness','Treat as a state machine with explicit residual thresholds and rollback.'),
('Depth-correct mixing with RealityKit entities','High','Two render pipelines need coherent depth/occlusion','Start with AR mesh occlusion + compositing; investigate RealityKit LowLevelMesh route for tighter integration.'),
('Dynamic / changing splat environment','High','Updating topology/appearance while maintaining stable registration','Defer until static world-locked overlay is reliable.'),
('On-device splat training','High','Unified-memory pressure, thermal limits, battery, latency','Mac-first training; on-device only as optional future capability.'),
], widths=[1.55,1.1,2.25,2.55])

add_callout(doc,'Practical assessment','The incremental difficulty of “one more splat” is not severe if each splat is already registered and can be culled independently. The hard part is the first robust bridge between ARKit world space and reconstructed splat space. Once that contract is stable, additional local overlays become a resource-management problem rather than a new geometry problem.','EAF3EF')

# 9 rendering integration options
h=doc.add_heading('9. RealityKit / Metal Integration Options', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
add_table(doc,['Option','Description','Pros','Cons','Decision'],[
('A. Parallel Metal splat renderer','RealityKit handles semantic entities; a custom Metal renderer draws splats using synchronized camera transforms.','Fastest path; mature splat code reusable; full renderer control.','Depth/compositing integration requires deliberate work.','Recommended v1'),
('B. RealityKit-native splats','Bake splat quads into LowLevelMesh, shade with CustomMaterial, GPU-sort indices.','One scene/depth pipeline; natural entity transforms.','Less proven on iOS; GSKit reference currently macOS-focused; may hit RealityKit constraints.','Investigate in parallel'),
('C. Web renderer embedded in native app','Reuse WebGL/WebGPU splat viewer in a web view.','Very fast demo.','Poor native scene/physics integration; awkward camera/depth sharing.','Prototype only'),
], widths=[1.35,1.75,1.7,1.85,1.0], font_size=8.6)

p=doc.add_paragraph('Apple’s `LowLevelMesh` is particularly relevant because it allows custom vertex formats and GPU-updated mesh data, while `CustomMaterial` exposes Metal surface/geometry shader hooks inside RealityKit. That combination is the basis of GSKit’s experimental RealityKit-native path and is worth tracking as the likely long-term unification route.')

# 10 self hosted model
h=doc.add_heading('10. Self-Hosted World-Model / Reconstruction Node', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
p=doc.add_paragraph('The “small self-hosted Genie-style world model” should be implemented as a local service around explicit scene state rather than as a monolithic video generator. The service can ingest camera frames, scene graph state, telemetry and user intent; propose state transitions or reconstructed appearance; then return typed scene deltas. Deterministic physics remains authoritative for mechanical behavior.')
add_code_block(doc,
'''Observations\n  camera frames / AR poses / scene mesh / telemetry / user actions\n        |\n        v\nPerception + reconstruction\n  object identity / splat / proxy geometry / semantic graph updates\n        |\n        v\nWorld-state model\n  predict / hypothesize / complete / simulate candidates\n        |\n        v\nPhysics + rule validation\n        |\n        v\nSceneDelta\n  transforms / state / annotations / splat-layer version / confidence''')

p=doc.add_paragraph('Cosine’s Genie report is useful here as an agent-loop analogy rather than as a world-rendering technology: it emphasizes planning, retrieval, code writing, and execution as separable processes. The analogous GMRI loop is observe/retrieve relevant state -> plan state change -> simulate/validate -> publish a bounded scene delta.')

# 11 security & provenance
h=doc.add_heading('11. Provenance, Safety, and Operational Integrity', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
add_bullets(doc,[
'Every spatial entity and splat layer should retain source provenance, timestamp, coordinate-frame identifier, and confidence.',
'Never let a generated world-model update silently overwrite authoritative telemetry or capture geometry; generated state is a separate provenance class.',
'Registration confidence is first-class state. A visually convincing but misregistered splat is operationally worse than no overlay.',
'Persist local captures and reconstructed scenes using explicit project boundaries; avoid accidental capture of unrelated personal content.',
'The God’s Eye View fork already distinguishes source-derived and modeled/estimated data; preserve that discipline across the native bridge.'
])

# 12 module layout
h=doc.add_heading('12. Proposed Codebase Layout', level=1); keep_with_next(h)
add_code_block(doc,
'''GMRI-Spatial/\n  Apps/\n    SpatialWorkbench-iOS/\n    SpatialWorkbench-macOS/\n  Packages/\n    SpatialCore/              # ids, transforms, semantic graph, state machine\n    SpatialTransport/         # WebSocket, schemas, snapshots/deltas\n    SpatialGeo/               # WGS84/ECEF/ENU math\n    SpatialPhysics/           # RealityKit physics adapters\n    SpatialExplode/           # assembly hierarchy + explode controller\n    SpatialCapture/           # ARKit capture, poses, intrinsics, mesh export\n    SpatialSplat/             # renderer protocol + MetalSplatter adapter\n    SpatialRegistration/      # Sim(3), ICP refinement, confidence metrics\n    SpatialWorldModelClient/  # local model service contract\n  Services/\n    gev-spatial-gateway/      # added beside existing God’s Eye View runtime\n    reconstruction-node/      # Mac-side training/alignment service\n  Specs/\n    spatial-state.schema.*\n    registration-state.md\n    provenance.md''')

p=doc.add_paragraph('The existing `oldmangrizzz/gods-eye-view` repository does not need to be rewritten. The smallest integration surface is a new gateway module that reads the existing data-manager/entity state and publishes the normalized spatial contract. Keeping that gateway narrow also makes it possible to upstream or rebase the fork without entangling native Apple code with the Cesium application.')

The resulting design is Apple-native: **Swift/SwiftUI + RealityKit + ARKit + Metal**, with the Mac acting as the heavier reconstruction/training/orchestration node where appropriate, and iPhone/iPad acting as the live spatial capture and interaction endpoints. That also preserves the WGS84→local ENU concept already present in your Ambient Spatial Cockpit work, rather than inventing a second coordinate architecture. fileciteturn0file1L198-L230 Your existing reconstruction stack already anticipates Gaussian splatting/Nerfstudio-style scene representations, so this is an extension of that work rather than a replacement. fileciteturn0file1L64-L95

I also dug specifically into the **additional Gaussian-splat/local-overlay problem**. The good news is that Apple's ecosystem is considerably further along here than I initially expected. `MetalSplatter` is already a Swift/Metal renderer targeting iOS/iPadOS/macOS and supporting PLY/SPZ/.splat, while `splatx-metal` goes substantially further into Apple-native 3DGS training/rendering and Apple-Silicon workflows. citeturn667191search0turn667191search6 I also found a RealityKit-native experiment using `LowLevelMesh` plus `CustomMaterial`, which is especially relevant if we eventually want splats, semantic entities, and depth behavior to live in a tighter unified render path rather than as separate compositors. citeturn667191search9

The document treats your **“Bridge Crossing”** point as a first-class subsystem: the moment a reconstructed splat is demonstrably registered into the live ARKit world frame. It defines capture → reconstruction → candidate registration → verification → bridged → degraded/re-registration, instead of simply eyeballing the overlay until it appears aligned. That is probably the single most technically important piece for the local-environment overlay you have in mind.

My difficulty assessment ended up roughly like this: adding another static splat after that registration contract exists is only **moderate**; multiple simultaneously registered splats become **moderate-to-high** because of memory and transparency/depth ordering; reliable Bridge Crossing itself is **high but tractable**; genuinely depth-correct interoperation between RealityKit geometry and an independent splat renderer is **high**; and continuously changing/dynamic splat environments are **high**. The recommendation is deliberately to let the ARKit scene mesh remain collision/occlusion authority at first while the splat is the high-fidelity visual layer.

I also inspected **your actual `oldmangrizzz/gods-eye-view` fork** and designed against its current CesiumJS/DataLayerManager/scene architecture. I did **not** alter the repository. The proposed integration keeps that project as the macro/global world plane and introduces a narrow spatial-state gateway into the Apple runtime rather than trying to port Cesium wholesale into RealityKit.

The final system can still become more native afterward, but the thing you take to New Mexico should already contain the actual God's Eye View system, the local spatial layer, interactive object state, and an on-device control model.

The key adjustment is that **God's Eye View is no longer merely a data provider**. Your existing fork becomes an actual first-class runtime inside the application.

For this week's build, I would package the existing Cesium/Vite client and host it directly in a `WKWebView`. That sounds less glamorous than rewriting Cesium into RealityKit, but it buys us something much more valuable before Thursday: **your complete existing GEV experience survives intact**—layers, camera behavior, tracking, telemetry, annotations, HUD, scene director, etc.—while Swift gains a bidirectional bridge into it.

Your fork already exposes the important objects through `window.__godsEyeView`: viewer, data manager, scene director, map controller, annotations and related runtime pieces. That's almost begging to be bridged instead of rewritten.

On your model idea: **Cactus Needle is actually a very strong fit for the interactive-state layer.**

I pulled the current `cactus-compute/needle` repository rather than relying on the name. Needle 3 is explicitly designed around **tool calls and structured extraction**, and it is tiny: the project describes deployable binaries in roughly the 8–29 MB range. More importantly for us, it deliberately returns an empty tool list instead of inventing an action when no tool matches, and its generation is constrained against the schemas you give it. citeturn445493search0turn445493search1

That is almost exactly what I want between human language and the world state.

I would **not make Needle the physics engine or world model**.

I'd make it the local intent → deterministic-action translator.

For example, you say:

> Pull the hydraulic system apart but leave the pump mounted, then show me where pressure is being lost.

Needle sees tools something like:

```text
explode_assembly(
    assembly_id,
    amount,
    exclude_components[]
)

set_component_state(
    component_id,
    state
)

highlight_flow(
    system_id,
    property,
    threshold
)

set_physics_enabled(
    component_id,
    enabled
)
```

It returns typed calls.

Then **our state machine** performs those operations.

That's dramatically safer and more deterministic than asking a general LLM to maintain the scene itself.

And Needle has a second advantage for the trip: Cactus explicitly supports local deployment and has a macOS ARM64 target today. The current project also supports local fine-tuning and structured tool definitions. citeturn445493search0

So we can start completely generic:

```text
"explode that engine halfway"
              ↓
Needle
              ↓
{
  tool: "set_explosion",
  assembly_id: "engine",
  amount: 0.5
}
              ↓
World State Manager
              ↓
RealityKit transforms
```

And later fine-tune it around **your vocabulary**.

That is much more interesting than stuffing a 7B model into the interaction loop.

### Layla is a different animal

I also investigated Layla.

If you're referring to `PapaKoftes/Layla`, it isn't really a model in the same sense. It's a **local agent framework** that hosts GGUF models, provides memory, tool dispatch, planning, approvals, browser automation, etc. It exposes an HTTP/OpenAI-compatible interface and is designed as a full personal/engineering agent. citeturn247533search0turn247533search2

There are two reasons I wouldn't use it in the critical path this week.

First, it's considerably more machinery than we need for interactive spatial state.

Second, the repo explicitly says it uses a **non-commercial source license**, not an OSI open-source license. citeturn247533search0

That's not automatically fatal for research work, but I would not weld GMRI's core spatial architecture to a license like that when something purpose-built and permissively licensed can do the function we actually need.

I'd instead think of Layla-like architecture later as a **macOS supervisory agent**:

```text
                   GMRI World
                      │
           ┌──────────┴─────────┐
           │                    │
     Needle control       larger agent
     reflex layer         reasoning layer
           │                    │
       milliseconds          seconds+
```

Needle is the spinal cord.

A larger model is the cortex.

Physics/state is reality.

That's the division I want.

## And I would slightly change the Gaussian-splat plan for Thursday

Because of the deadline, we should **not require live local 3DGS training on the mobile device** to call the system functional.

The renderer is the critical thing.

We already found a very credible Apple-native path. `MetalSplatter` renders PLY/SPZ/.splat directly using Swift/Metal across iOS, iPadOS and macOS. There are also newer experimental Apple-native renderers, including a RealityKit `LowLevelMesh` approach and Metal renderers supporting multiple sorting strategies. The really interesting long-term project is `splatx-metal`, because it moves actual 3DGS training into Metal and exposes Apple-native deployment paths.

For **Thursday**, I would establish this contract:

```text
ARKit local world
       │
       ├── authoritative anchors
       ├── scene geometry/depth
       ├── RealityKit objects
       │
       └── RegisteredSplatLayer[]
                  │
                  ├── transform
                  ├── source
                  ├── confidence
                  ├── timestamp
                  ├── opacity
                  ├── visibility
                  └── registration state
```

Then your unique local overlay becomes just another registered spatial layer.

You can have:

```text
Physical room
   +
ARKit geometry
   +
Splat: baseline reconstruction
   +
Splat: your special overlay
   +
semantic objects
   +
God's Eye View geographic context
```

all occupying the same coordinate system.

That is the foundation your later **Bridge Crossing** logic needs.

Not a mockup.

Not screenshots.

A real application in which:

1. **Your full God's Eye View fork runs inside the Apple application.**

3. GEV can send selected/global entities into the native state bus.

The other thing your correction changes is how I would define the Thursday gate. I would make the build pass a real **field-readiness burn-in matrix**, not a feature checklist.

Something along these lines:

| Failure we intentionally cause | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| Kill app mid-session | clean state recovery |
| Kill GEV web runtime | native shell stays alive and restarts it |
| Drop network | local XR and cached state continue |
| Restore network | resync without duplicate state |
| Unplug glasses | application survives |
| Reconnect glasses | rendering resumes automatically |
| Power-cycle Beam | rejoins without manual reconfiguration |
| Corrupt a splat load | reject layer, keep world alive |
| Huge splat / memory pressure | degrade LOD, do not terminate |
| Bad tool call from Needle | schema rejection, no scene mutation |
| Physics instability | isolate offending object/subsystem |
| ARKit relocalization loss | mark registration degraded, don't fake precision |
| JavaScript bridge exception | bridge reports fault, native side remains stable |
| Background/foreground iOS app | state restored |
| Thermal pressure | shed expensive layers predictably |
| Low battery | reduce compute before OS kills us |
| 2–4 hour continuous use | no progressive memory growth |
| rapid mode switching | no stale render/state ownership |
| repeated forced crashes | deterministic recovery every time |

That is much closer to the engineering culture you’re describing than calling something “MVP complete.”

And I think the **preventability standard** is the right organizing principle for the software architecture too:

> Any failure mode we can reasonably anticipate before deployment is a design input, not an excuse afterward.

That means fault containment becomes part of the design.

The Gaussian renderer should be a separate layer owner. If a malformed SPZ/PLY causes an allocation or decode failure, that layer disappears—not the world.

Needle should never mutate scene state directly. It proposes typed operations; the state manager validates them.

The Beam should never hold unique state. If it bricks, swap the puck.

That is how I would interpret your “if I hurt it, it wasn’t put together correctly” requirement in system terms.

### The Apple Sandbox actually helps in one respect

It forces you into clean service boundaries.

Every capability has to be granted explicitly through entitlements, extensions, App Groups, framework permissions, or interprocess mechanisms. That can become your equivalent of a microkernel capability model.

Instead of trying to defeat the sandbox:

```text
Responder OS
     ↓
"give me all system access"
```

you exploit it:

```text
Responder OS Core

 ├─ Spatial capability
 ├─ Health capability
 ├─ Motion capability
 ├─ Network capability
 ├─ Portal capability
 ├─ Storage capability
 ├─ Accessibility capability
 └─ External-device capability
```

Each service knows exactly what Apple permission/entitlement backs it.

That is much more defensible and maintainable.

Apple also has a whole managed-app/device-management architecture where configuration and secrets can be provisioned into managed applications and extensions. Yep. I went and looked at the actual **Laya** you meant instead of guessing.

And yes: there is absolutely a place where **Laya fits better than Cactus Needle**.

Laya is a very different animal. It is a non-autoregressive **System 1 decision engine**. You give it some state—text, JSON, a ticket, an event description—and ask typed questions. It returns `choice`, `score`, or yes/no-style probability outputs with calibrated confidence, all in one forward pass. It deliberately does **not** generate prose. citeturn946692search4turn946692search8

That makes it particularly interesting for the system you’re building because a lot of what an XR operating layer needs is not “generate language.” It is:

**What state am I in? What mode should I enter? Which input should I trust? How confident am I? Should this action be accepted, rejected, or escalated?**

That is much closer to Laya’s design than Needle’s.

Needle, meanwhile, is very explicitly optimized for **tool calling, structured extraction, embeddings, and tiny-device deployment**. Cactus says the binary can be roughly 8–29 MB depending on depth, and it is designed for mobiles, wearables, robots, microcontrollers, etc. It is excellent at mapping something like “open the hydraulic assembly and highlight the pump” into the right schema-constrained function call. citeturn946692search4

So I would not choose between them. I’d use them for different jobs.

| Function | Better fit |
|---|---|
| “What action did Grizz ask for?” | **Needle** |
| Fill arguments for a tool call | **Needle** |
| Fast local voice → command pipeline | **Needle + Whistle** |
| “Which tracking source should currently be trusted?” | **Laya** |
| “Is this localization degraded enough to fall back?” | **Laya** |

## Scope

Evaluate current open image-generation models in roughly the 0.6B–8B class for the GMRI lab's available local hardware:

- 2017 iMac / Proxmox 9 / Radeon Pro 570 4 GB / 32 GB RAM.
- 2022 MacBook Air M2 / 8 GB unified memory.
- RunPod and cloud retained as overflow, not the default path.

The goal is not to pick the newest model. It is to identify the strongest practical local-first stack under tight VRAM/RAM and operating-cost constraints.

## Findings

### 1. Z-Image-Turbo is the strongest first target for the Radeon/Proxmox path

The official Tongyi-MAI model is Apache-2.0 and uses a Qwen3 text encoder. The reference BF16 repository is very large, but stable-diffusion.cpp explicitly documents Z-Image operation on GPUs with 4 GB of VRAM or less using quantized GGUF weights and a Qwen3-4B text encoder.

Primary sources:
- https://huggingface.co/Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo
- https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp/blob/master/docs/z_image.md

Why it fits:
- Quantized GGUF path.
- Vulkan backend available in stable-diffusion.cpp.
- Explicit 4 GB VRAM guidance.
- Apache-2.0 upstream model.
- Small enough text encoder family to remain inside GMRI's normal local model budget.

### 2. FLUX.2 [klein] 4B is the best second model to validate

Black Forest Labs publishes FLUX.2 [klein] 4B under Apache-2.0. It supports both text-to-image and image editing. stable-diffusion.cpp added FLUX.2-klein support in January 2026.

Primary sources:
- https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-klein-4B
- https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp

Important constraint:
- The official repository is 23.7 GB total and the BF16 single-file transformer is 7.75 GB, so the stock weights are not a 4 GB VRAM fit. The practical question is quantized Vulkan behavior on the Pro 570, which must be benchmarked locally before making it the default.

### 3. SANA-Sprint 1.6B is the efficiency candidate, but the runtime path is less convenient for the Pro 570

SANA-Sprint 1.6B is Apache-2.0, generates at 1024 px, supports 1–4-step inference and ControlNet, and uses Gemma2-2B-IT as its text encoder. NVIDIA reports very strong speed/quality efficiency on modern NVIDIA hardware.

Primary sources:
- https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Sana_Sprint_1.6B_1024px
- https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/api/pipelines/sana_sprint

Why it is not first:
- It is not currently listed among stable-diffusion.cpp's supported image architectures.
- Its best-documented path is Diffusers/PyTorch, which is less attractive on an older Polaris AMD GPU under Linux.
- It remains worth testing on Apple MPS and/or CPU as an alternate low-parameter renderer.

### 4. Lumina-Image 2.0 is a credible 2B-class fallback

Lumina-Image 2.0 is a 2B, Apache-2.0 flow-based image model with Diffusers support and documented CPU offload.

Primary source:
- https://huggingface.co/Alpha-VLLM/Lumina-Image-2.0

It is interesting for low-parameter experimentation, but it lacks the same 4 GB Vulkan deployment story Z-Image currently has.

### 5. Qwen-Image 2.1 is within the transformer's nominal 7B class, but the complete runtime is heavier

Hugging Face currently lists Qwen-Image 2.1 as a 7B text-to-image model. stable-diffusion.cpp has day-0 support, but its documented pipeline uses Qwen3-VL-8B as the text encoder plus the Qwen image model and VAE.

Primary sources:
- https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1
- https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp/blob/master/docs/qwen_image_2.1.md

Conclusion:
- It stays in the research pool, but should not be the first 4 GB Radeon target.
- Quantized CPU/RAM offload may make it usable, but that must be measured rather than assumed.

### 6. Older FLUX.1 is not a good fit for the stated 2B–8B local budget

FLUX.1 Schnell is a 12B transformer. stable-diffusion.cpp can make it run on 4–6 GB VRAM with quantization, but it violates the lab's preferred local parameter ceiling and offers less reason to accept that cost now that FLUX.2-klein 4B and Z-Image exist.

Primary sources:
- https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-schnell
- https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp/blob/master/docs/flux.md

## Recommended local stack

### Proxmox / Radeon Pro 570
1. stable-diffusion.cpp
2. Vulkan backend
3. Z-Image-Turbo quantized GGUF as the default model
4. FLUX.2-klein 4B quantized as the second model after validation
5. CPU/RAM offload where needed
6. Embedded web UI/API as the local access surface

### M2 MacBook Air
- Keep image generation secondary because it is an 8 GB fanless field/development machine.
- Test SANA-Sprint 1.6B through MPS and/or lightweight Apple-native runtimes.
- Do not make sustained image generation a required background workload.

### Overflow
- RunPod for high-resolution, batch, or models that are inefficient locally.
- Cloud generation only as a reserve path.

## Acceptance benchmark before choosing defaults

Run the same fixed prompt suite across candidate models and record:
- cold-start time
- first-image time
- steady-state 512 and 1024 generation time
- peak VRAM
- peak host RAM
- thermal stability over 10 consecutive generations
- text rendering quality
- photorealism
- diagram/technical illustration quality
- prompt adherence
- image-edit fidelity
- crash/recovery behavior

Do not pick the default solely from leaderboard scores. Pick the model that produces useful GMRI output reliably on the actual hardware.

So if I were building this on your actual budget, I would test in this order:

1. **Z-Image-Turbo quantized GGUF on Proxmox + Radeon/Vulkan**
2. **FLUX.2 klein 4B quantized on the same stack**
3. **SANA-Sprint 1.6B on the M2 or alternate local runtime**

6. Cloud/RunPod only when the local stack cannot satisfy the job

That gives you **local-first, cloud-reserve**, without pretending the lab owns hardware it does not.

Yes. And there are two separate points here.

First: the model you linked is **not an image model by itself**. It is a collection of **uncensored Qwen3-family text encoders** intended to be dropped into image pipelines such as **FLUX Klein, Z-Image Turbo, and Anima**. The model card says exactly that, and the repo contains separate 0.6B, 4B, 8B, and VL-4B GGUF encoder files. citeturn410248view0 citeturn459410view0

That is actually useful for your purpose because it means we do not have to find a fully “uncensored everything” image stack as one monolith. We can deliberately build the stack from components:

```text
prompt
  ↓
uncensored Qwen3 text encoder
  ↓
image model
  ↓
VAE / decode
  ↓
output
```

And for Z-Image specifically, the repo includes a **Qwen3-4B-ZImage-Heretic-Genesis-Q8.gguf** around 4.28 GB. citeturn459410view0

Your Hugging Face search also shows that there are now quite a few uncensored Qwen-Image 2.1 derivatives, so this is not some one-off fringe path. The top of your results includes multiple 7B uncensored Qwen-Image 2.1 models, and the LuffyTheFox encoder repo appears right there among them. fileciteturn105file0L7-L22 fileciteturn105file0L27-L44

For EMS-adjacent research, your reasoning is sound: if the workflow may need to generate or edit clinically unpleasant imagery, trauma, exposed anatomy, burns, wounds, disaster scenes, etc., then having the local stack silently refuse categories of medically relevant content is a real operational problem. Building the local stack around models and encoders that do not impose those restrictions from the beginning avoids having two separate toolchains.

Now, on **ComfyUI versus Stable Diffusion**:

You do not actually have to choose between those.

**ComfyUI is the orchestration/runtime interface. Stable Diffusion is one family of image models.**

ComfyUI can run:
- Stable Diffusion
- SDXL
- SD3.5
- FLUX
- FLUX.2
- Qwen Image
- Z-Image
- Lumina
- Anima
- a bunch of other image/video/3D models

The current ComfyUI README explicitly lists Qwen Image, Z-Image, Flux.1, Flux.2, Lumina Image 2.0, Anima, and many others as supported model families. It also specifically says it is designed for low-memory local hardware and can run large models with **4 GB VRAM + 8 GB RAM** using weight streaming and offload. citeturn0fetch0

So for your lab, **ComfyUI is probably the better front end**.

Especially because you said this is an area where you do not already have a lot of preset knowledge.

The visual node graph lets you build one workflow once and then expose only the controls you actually care about. ComfyUI now has **App Mode**, which can turn a complicated node graph into a much simpler operator-facing interface. citeturn0fetch0

That means you could make yourself something like:

```text
GMRI Image Console

Prompt: [...........................]

Mode:
[Clinical] [Technical] [Photoreal] [Diagram]

Model:
[Z-Image] [Flux Klein] [Qwen]

Resolution:
[512] [768] [1024]

[GENERATE]
```

while the ugly node graph sits behind it.

That strikes me as much better than forcing you to manually manipulate a complicated diffusion pipeline every time.

And importantly, **ComfyUI-GGUF exists specifically to run quantized transformer image models in ComfyUI**. Its whole purpose is loading GGUF diffusion models and GGUF text encoders on low-end hardware. It explicitly supports GGUF UNET/model loading and quantized T5/text encoders. citeturn0fetch1

That opens the door to exactly the kind of stack you are considering:

```text
ComfyUI
  │
  ├── Z-Image Turbo GGUF
  │      +
  │   Qwen3-4B uncensored encoder GGUF
  │
  ├── FLUX.2 klein
  │      +
  │   Qwen3 uncensored encoder
  │
  └── future models
```

There is one important caveat with your Radeon Pro 570.

The official ComfyUI Linux AMD path assumes **PyTorch + ROCm**. ComfyUI does mention an override path for unsupported/older AMD GPUs, but your Polaris card is old enough that I would not assume a clean PyTorch/ROCm experience just because GPU passthrough itself works. citeturn0fetch0

That is where the choice gets interesting.

For the **Radeon Pro 570**, I would test two execution paths:

```text
Path A
ComfyUI
↓
PyTorch / ROCm
↓
Radeon Pro 570

Path B
ComfyUI as operator UI
↓
stable-diffusion.cpp backend
↓
Vulkan
↓
Radeon Pro 570
```

Path B may end up being the more reliable way to exploit that card.

Because `stable-diffusion.cpp` has a much stronger low-VRAM/Vulkan story on old AMD hardware than PyTorch does.

So I would not throw out stable-diffusion.cpp.

I would put **ComfyUI in front of it**.

That gives you the easier visual interface while keeping the runtime that is more likely to cooperate with the Polaris GPU.

In other words:

```text
you
 ↓
ComfyUI
 ↓
workflow / model selection
 ↓
backend
 ├── native Comfy/PyTorch if it behaves
 └── stable-diffusion.cpp/Vulkan if that behaves better
 ↓
Radeon Pro 570
```

That is the architecture I would test.

And the linked LuffyTheFox encoder fits neatly into it.

For your first benchmark stack, I would probably try:

1. **Z-Image Turbo + Qwen3-4B ZImage Heretic/Genesis encoder**
2. **FLUX.2 klein + compatible uncensored Qwen3 encoder**

So yes: **ComfyUI is not only viable; I think it is probably the better operational layer for you than working directly with stable-diffusion.cpp.** The latter can remain the engine underneath if the Polaris card prefers Vulkan over ROCm.

You’ve mostly been studying the **cognition layer**: reasoning, agency, alignment, consciousness questions, generality, governance, global effects. Imaging, audio, spatial computing, sensors, embodiment, etc. are much closer to the rest of the nervous system and body.

And that explains why ComfyUI was a useful missing piece conceptually. It is not “the image intelligence” in the same way an LLM is the intelligence. It is more like an **orchestration fabric for visual subsystems**: encoder, generative model, conditioning, masks, depth, ControlNet, upscalers, segmentation, image editing, and eventually video/3D can all be assembled into a workflow.

Audio has almost exactly the same decomposition:

```text
hearing
microphone
    ↓
signal processing / VAD
    ↓
speech recognition
    ↓
language / reasoning
    ↓
decision / tool execution
    ↓
speech synthesis
    ↓
speaker
```

And then the spatial work we’ve been discussing adds:

```text
vision                    proprioception
camera / depth            IMU / Watch / UWB
      ↓                         ↓
perception              pose estimation
      └─────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
             world model
                ↓
          reasoning / action
                ↓
    XR rendering / physical action
```

The interesting part is that once those systems are connected, **the core model does not have to personally be good at every modality**.

That is probably the architectural trap worth avoiding.

You don’t necessarily want one enormous multimodal model doing:

> see → hear → localize → reason → make image → speak → control portal → remember everything.

That creates one expensive, opaque failure domain.

What you can build instead is closer to a biological arrangement: specialized systems feeding a common state.

For the components we’ve already found:

- **Needle** — fast language → action/tool reflex.
- **Laya** — quick classification, state assessment, routing and confidence.
- **larger LLM/cloud model** — slower deliberative cognition.
- **Whistle or another STT model** — hearing.
- **TTS model** — voice.
- **ComfyUI + image models** — visual imagination / synthesis.
- **vision models** — visual perception.
- **ARKit + conventional fusion math** — proprioception/localization.
- **God’s Eye View** — extended situational awareness beyond immediate perception.
- **Gaussian splats / spatial reconstruction** — environmental representation.
- **Responder/GMRI operating layer** — integration between all those pieces.

Which gets remarkably close to your “missing body parts” observation without requiring us to settle any philosophical question about what the resulting thing *is*.

And there is a practical consequence for how we should research the rest of this.

We should probably stop searching for **“the best AI model”** and start building a **capability map**:

  depth

  image editing

AUDIO

OUTPUT / ACTION

```

Then, for every box, we find the **smallest good local model or deterministic system that can do the job**, and escalate outward only when necessary:

**local deterministic → local small model → local larger model → home compute → RunPod → cloud.**

That would fit both your technical constraints and the economic reality of a self-funded lab substantially better than trying to imitate how a venture-funded lab builds a multimodal system.

The audio pieces that immediately matter to us are:

```text
your family audio

speaker/accent-adapted ASR
        ↓
raw transcript + confidence
        ↓
S1-mini / cleanup layer
        ↓
final text

Each adapter could learn pronunciation, pacing, local vowel patterns, names, EMS vocabulary, habitual contractions, and each person’s characteristic DFW speech without duplicating the whole model.

You’re thinking of **Voz**.

Its distinctive feature is exactly what you remembered: it gives a **start and end timestamp for every word**, with about **80 ms frame resolution**. Desert Ant even describes it as giving “a start and an end on every word.” citeturn996123search1turn996123search5

So the pairing you’re proposing is actually interesting:

```text
audio
  ↓
Clear
  ↓
MacParakeet
  ↓
Voz timing/alignment signal
  ↓
transcript + word boundaries
```

I would modify that slightly, though, because **Voz is itself an ASR model**, not merely a boundary detector. So rather than blindly serializing Voz after MacParakeet, I’d use them as **parallel recognizers** and let Voz contribute its timestamp information and second-opinion transcript.

Something more like:

```text
                 ┌─ MacParakeet transcript
audio → Clear ───┤
                 └─ Voz transcript + per-word start/end
                         ↓
                 alignment / reconciliation
                         ↓
                 final transcript
```

That gives us something much more valuable than either model alone.

If both recognize the same word, confidence goes up. If MacParakeet says one thing but Voz hears another, the system knows **that word deserves attention instead of silently committing to one interpretation**.

And because Voz provides those word boundaries, we can go back to the actual audio slice around the disputed word instead of reprocessing the whole utterance.

For example:

```text
MacParakeet: "I'm leaving the store"
Voz:         "I'm leaving the store"

→ accept

MacParakeet: "I just got done fucking your mom..."
Voz:         "I'm leaving the store"

→ disagreement detected
→ re-evaluate corresponding audio spans
→ do not send message automatically
```

That starts getting us much closer to the failure behavior you actually want: **uncertainty should create friction, not confidence**.

One more Desert Ant component may eventually be useful too: **Align**. It refines word timestamps, although right now it specifically attaches to Apple's `SpeechAnalyzer`, not arbitrary ASR engines, so it is not directly a MacParakeet postprocessor. citeturn996123search6

So yes: **Clear + MacParakeet + Voz in parallel** is a much more promising architecture than replacing MacParakeet outright. And because MacParakeet already works acceptably most of the time for you, we can spend compute specifically on the 10% where the recognizers disagree instead of trying to make every utterance pass through a giant model.

Exactly. That is the move.

The interesting part isn’t “two ASR models are better than one” in some generic ensemble sense. It’s that **they fail differently**, and that gives us a usable signal.

MacParakeet can be the primary transcript path because you already know it behaves well most of the time. Voz can run beside it as the independent second witness with word-level timing. Then we compare not only the strings, but the aligned spans.

If they agree closely, accept with high confidence. If they disagree on a low-impact word, maybe accept with a flag. If they disagree on something semantically consequential—names, numbers, navigation instructions, medication terms, profanity, negation, destinations, commands—kick just that audio slice back through another pass or ask for confirmation.

**one monitor can lie; independent corroboration changes confidence.**

And because Voz gives us timing boundaries, the disagreement doesn’t have to trigger a whole-utterance retry. We can isolate the 300–800 ms region around the disputed word and spend extra compute only there.

The next layer I’d add after that is not another full ASR model immediately. Then Laya answers something closer to:

interpretation_confidence: 0.63
semantic_risk: 0.92
action: ASK

candidate_b: "turn west on Rosedale"
```

That is much better than handing the disagreement to a generative LLM and saying, “What do you think Grizz meant?”

Especially because Laya supports **typed choices, numerical scores, confidence and abstention**. So we can explicitly train/calibrate around three outputs:

**ACCEPT / REPROCESS / ASK**

And those don’t need identical thresholds.

For example, a transcript could have 91% overall confidence but still produce `ASK` because the disagreement concerns **left versus right**. Conversely, maybe 76% confidence on whether you said “the” versus “a” can just pass.

So there are really two probabilities:

**How likely is this transcription correct?**

and

**How costly is it if this transcription is wrong?**

Laya can operate over both instead of pretending confidence alone represents risk.

```text

      ↓
tiny arbitration model
      ↓
ACCEPT | REPROCESS | ASK
```

At that point it could become ridiculously small because it doesn’t need English competence in the broad sense. It needs to recognize **ASR disagreement patterns + consequence classes**.

**AppLess is not really “an app launcher without icons.”** The useful concept is that the interface is **generated around the current intent**, in native components, at the moment of need. No fixed app hierarchy, no permanent menu tree, no requirement that the user first decide which software silo contains the capability they want.

Interaction with that generated surface then causes the next surface to be generated, with likely destinations prefetched. The model is constrained by a component contract and emits a compact UI DSL that gets rendered as native UI.

Yes. That clarifies the architecture in a way that matters for the PRD.

The important separation is:

**Operating system ≠ intelligence ≠ tool.**

GrizzOS is the proof-of-concept operating environment. ResponderOS is the broader destination. CompanionOS is one implementation layer around capability routing and device access. Atlas contributes navigation/situational-awareness concepts. Dottie/Donny-class systems are intelligences. Leia/Cactus-class systems can be highly capable tools or specialized cognitive components. The point is that none of them gets to absorb the others.

That separation is already visible in your repos. CompanionOS has a **Capability Bus** specifically separating media/comms/actions/notes/search from whichever provider or model is handling a request, and it already uses Convex for persistence rather than treating the model as the state substrate. GrizzOS likewise describes itself as the operating-system layer and uses Convex, voice, telemetry, rendering, and spatial managers as infrastructure around the intelligence. The older Atlas/ResponderOS spec is also explicitly model-agnostic and treats navigation, perception, tools, and policy as separate callable capabilities.

The part that changes the UI discussion is your last point.

For the **human-facing UI**, the primary intelligence does **not** need to be Dottie.

It can be a much smaller, faster local interaction intelligence whose job is basically:

**intent → capability selection → interface generation → result presentation**

That could be Leia, Cactus, Laya, or a blend, depending on what exact role each one proves best at.

Then Dottie remains available **through** the operating environment when the task actually warrants Dottie-level reasoning, watch judgment, provenance analysis, dissent, or escalation.

So the UI architecture starts looking more like:

**Human / Digital Intelligence**  
↕  
**Interaction Intelligence** — fast, local, low-latency  
↕  
**GrizzOS capability/intent layer**  
↕  
**tools / navigation / GEV / sensors / storage / Dottie / other intelligences**

That fits your boundary argument much better than hanging the whole interface directly off one giant model.

And it solves another problem at the same time: the **same UI mechanism can serve both humans and digital intelligences**.

A person says:

> “Show me what changed around us.”

A digital intelligence can issue essentially the same semantic intent programmatically.

The OS decides which capabilities are needed, the lightweight interaction intelligence determines the appropriate presentation, and the user gets the minimum useful visual/spatial surface.

- Security groups aren't equivalent to AWS networking. Their EC2 guide specifically says the functional networking path currently uses the `default` security group in this mode, even though the API itself implements `CreateSecurityGroup`. citeturn169436view4
- Agent Office expects a **real reachable IP that it can SSH into** after AWS hands it a `PublicIpAddress`. LocalStack's “public IP” is effectively an address assigned to its Docker-backed instance. “Dramatically bigger hammer” means **OpenStack is not an AWS emulator in the same sense as LocalStack, LocalEmu, or Floci. It is an actual private-cloud operating system.**

Instead of pretending to be AWS just enough to satisfy software expecting AWS APIs, OpenStack gives you the machinery to build your own cloud: real virtual machines, virtual networks, floating IPs, images, block storage, identity, quotas, scheduling, APIs, and—optionally—an EC2 compatibility layer on top. OpenStack’s own architecture is a collection of independent services tied together through APIs, databases, and a message broker. citeturn953792search13turn953792search7

That difference is why I called it a bigger hammer.

At the small end, what we were discussing with LocalStack-like systems is approximately:

**Agent Office**
→ talks AWS EC2 API  
→ emulator translates that into Docker/container-ish resources  
→ Agent Office gets something sufficiently EC2-shaped to work.

With OpenStack, it becomes:

**Agent Office**
→ AWS EC2 API compatibility endpoint  
→ OpenStack control plane  
→ Nova schedules a real VM  
→ Neutron creates its actual virtual network interfaces/security rules/IPs  
→ Glance supplies its Ubuntu image  
→ Cinder can provide persistent block storage  
→ Keystone handles identity/authentication  
→ hypervisor actually boots the machine.

That is substantially closer to **“we own AWS”** than **“we fooled this program into thinking AWS exists.”**

OpenStack's EC2 compatibility service is specifically a standalone service designed to accept EC2/VPC API calls and translate them into OpenStack operations. It supports a pretty large portion of the EC2 surface Agent Office cares about: `RunInstances`, `StartInstances`, `StopInstances`, `TerminateInstances`, `CreateKeyPair`, security groups, `AllocateAddress`, `AssociateAddress`, `DescribeInstances`, VPC/subnet operations, volumes, images, tags, and more.         ├── tag it
        └── SSH in and provision Agent Office

An OpenStack deployment can provide **real equivalents** for essentially that entire conceptual flow.

AWS CLI

    │
┌──────────── OpenStack ──────────────┐
│                                     │
│ Keystone ─ identity                 │
│ Nova ───── compute / VM scheduling  │
│ Neutron ── networking               │
│ Glance ─── VM images                │
│ Cinder ─── block storage            │

## What all those OpenStack pieces actually do

You absolutely would **not** need every OpenStack project. There are dozens. The core useful ones are much smaller.

**Nova** is compute.

Nova receives something equivalent to:

> Launch me an instance of flavor X using image Y.

It doesn't itself run the VM. It schedules it to a compute node, generally using KVM/QEMU through libvirt.

On your hardware, that ultimately results in a real VM running on your CPU and RAM.

**Neutron** is networking.

This is where OpenStack starts getting considerably heavier than Proxmox plus Docker.

Neutron can create:

- isolated networks
- subnets
- routers
- security groups
- virtual interfaces
- floating/public IPs
- DHCP
- NAT
- tenant separation

Its networking subsystem isn't just “give container an IP.” It's designed for datacenter-scale multi-tenant virtual networking. OpenStack documents deployments with distinct management, guest, external, and API network domains. citeturn953792search7

For GMRI, much of that capability would initially be enormous overkill.

But it also means we could eventually say:

```text
Research network
Clinical sandbox network
Untrusted-agent network
Production services network
Development network
Internet-isolated network
```

and enforce those boundaries at infrastructure level.

**Glance** is the image catalog.

Instead of manually installing Ubuntu every time, you store images:

```text
Ubuntu 24.04
Debian
special GMRI agent host
ResponderOS test image
whatever
```

Then tell the cloud:

> Create three machines from this image.

**Cinder** is block storage.

Think AWS EBS.

VM disappears; its persistent disk can remain.

Volumes can be attached/detached independently of the VM lifecycle.

**Keystone** is identity.

Users, projects, roles, services, authentication.

This is another part that would initially look hilariously oversized for one guy in a lab—but it becomes useful if digital collaborators are eventually given **bounded infrastructure authority**.

Instead of:

> Here is root. Please don't fuck anything up.

you can eventually express:

> This identity may create compute in this project, inspect these resources, but cannot touch production networking or destroy persistent storage.

That part is potentially very relevant to your authority model.

**Placement** tracks resources.

CPUs, memory, resource inventories, allocations.

Nova uses it when deciding where something can run.

Add another physical compute machine later, and now OpenStack can decide:

> iMac is full; put this workload on box #2.

That's where “one weird old computer in the house” starts turning into an actual little cloud.

# Why it's so much heavier

Because once you install OpenStack, **you are the cloud provider.**

AWS has entire engineering divisions keeping EC2 functional.

OpenStack gives you the software those engineers would operate.

Even the relatively friendly Kolla-Ansible deployment path expects you to understand some amount of Linux networking, Ansible and containerized infrastructure. Its current quick-start requires at least two network interfaces, 8 GB RAM and 40 GB disk even for a basic deployment/evaluation system, and explicitly recommends familiarity with Ansible and Docker. citeturn953792search1

And that's the **minimum**, not “this will be pleasant with eight agents running.”

A real OpenStack environment introduces infrastructure components whose sole job is keeping the infrastructure running.

You're dealing with things like:

# The EC2 API is the important trick

The standalone OpenStack `ec2-api` service sits in front of OpenStack and accepts AWS-style requests.

OpenStack says that service assumes you already have at least:

- Compute
- Networking
- Block Storage
- Identity
- Image

running underneath it. citeturn533828search5

The EC2 endpoint traditionally listens separately—port **8788** by default—and translates EC2/VPC behavior into the OpenStack cloud beneath it. citeturn533828search1turn533828search8

So Agent Office's deployment script could theoretically be modified from:

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances ...
```

against AWS to:

```bash
aws --endpoint-url=http://our-openstack-ec2-api:8788 ec2 run-instances ...
```

with OpenStack credentials represented in the AWS credential mechanism expected by that compatibility service.

Then this:

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances
```

would eventually cause Nova to boot a **real KVM VM on our hardware**.

That's a radically different thing from LocalStack fabricating enough state to answer:

```json
{
  "InstanceId": "i-123456"
}
```

while associating it with a container.

# Where Agent Office might fight us

Its script is written around **AWS behavior**, not abstract EC2 semantics.

That means we'd need to audit individual assumptions.

For instance, Agent Office currently asks AWS for an instance type like:

```text
t3.xlarge
```

OpenStack doesn't intrinsically have AWS instance types.

OpenStack has **flavors**.

We could literally create a flavor corresponding to it:

```text
name: t3.xlarge
vCPU: 4
RAM: 16384 MB
disk: 50 GB
```

Depending on how the EC2 compatibility layer maps flavors/instance types, we either expose that name or adapt the script.

Agent Office expects an AWS Elastic IP.

OpenStack has **floating IPs**.

The EC2 layer supports `AllocateAddress` and `AssociateAddress`, so that translation exists. citeturn533828search0

Agent Office expects AWS security groups.

Neutron has security groups, and the compatibility API supports the corresponding EC2 operations.

Agent Office expects an AMI/image identifier.

OpenStack has Glance images. Again, that requires mapping.

Agent Office expects EC2 tags.

The compatibility API supports `CreateTags`. citeturn533828search0

Agent Office expects `DescribeInstanceTypes`.

This is one of the places we'd have to check carefully because OpenStack's EC2 compatibility isn't complete and the Agent Office deployment script uses instance-type architecture data when resizing. That could require a tiny adapter rather than pure endpoint replacement.

So this would not necessarily be:

**change endpoint, press button, victory.**

It could become:

**small compatibility shim around the Agent Office AWS deploy script.**

Still tractable.

The GMRI material already assumes a system where operating environment, intelligences, tools, sensors, state, and authority remain distinct, and where the environment mediates access to capabilities instead of collapsing everything into one application. fileciteturn174file2 That is exactly the kind of organization that eventually benefits from having **compute, storage, networking, identity, and resource authority exposed as services instead of as individual machines you babysit manually**.

The part that makes me take OpenStack seriously for GMRI is not “private AWS.” It is that you have several very different workloads that should probably not all live in the same undifferentiated infrastructure bucket:

- GrizOS operational services
- Dottie and other persistent intelligences
- transient coding/research agents
- disposable sandboxes
- local model inference
- storage and provenance systems
- geospatial/spatial services
- future ResponderOS and CompanionOS infrastructure
- research environments where something may intentionally be allowed to break
- production environments where it absolutely should not

That last distinction especially matters because your own design already says boundaries are explicit and that material actions/state changes carry provenance and authority state. fileciteturn174file2 A private cloud gives you somewhere to **enforce those distinctions below the application layer** instead of merely documenting them.

```

And the infrastructure decides where and how that exists.

That is **far more compatible with the organization you're describing** than “Dottie knows the hostname of the Proxmox box.”

There are a few reasons I think OpenStack deserves a real evaluation rather than immediate adoption.

First, **GMRI's scope is heterogeneous enough**. You are not building one SaaS application. You have local-first systems, spatial computing, AI workloads, research tooling, mobile/field systems, persistent services, burst compute, and systems with substantially different authority requirements. A cloud control plane becomes more valuable as the number of unlike workloads increases.

Second, **you care about sovereignty**. The GrizOS PRD explicitly requires real local capability rather than a shell that dies when connectivity disappears. fileciteturn174file2 Owning the control plane underneath your workloads fits that principle extremely well.

Third, **you already have hybrid compute**. You've got local hardware and burst GPU capacity rather than one uniform cluster. OpenStack won't magically unify every external provider, but it gives you an internal resource model around which you can build that larger abstraction.

Fourth, **authority is already a first-class design concept at GMRI**. OpenStack projects, roles, quotas, networks, and service identities could eventually map onto that in a meaningful way. Not one-to-one with Dottie's authority doctrine, but enough that the infrastructure itself can say, “this actor may create a sandbox but cannot destroy this volume or enter this network.”

And fifth, your PRD explicitly treats software and hardware choices as replaceable implementation details while preserving durable operating principles. fileciteturn174file2 That means using OpenStack would not require making **OpenStack itself** part of GrizOS's identity. It would remain substrate. If something better replaces it later, GrizOS should not care.

Where I would be cautious is **scale economics**.

OpenStack makes more architectural sense for GMRI than it presently makes hardware sense for your single 32 GB Proxmox iMac. Those are different questions.

Today, you could absolutely build a small contained OpenStack deployment and learn it. But if you tried to move everything into it immediately, you'd spend a stupid percentage of your available RAM running the control plane instead of research workloads.

So I would treat it as a **strategic infrastructure candidate**, not “tonight's migration target.”

The path I'd investigate would be:

```text
NOW
Proxmox remains the stable host
        │
        ├── current services
        ├── Agent Office
        └── small OpenStack laboratory

TEST
Can OpenStack provide:
- sane VM provisioning
- network isolation
- identity/authority controls
- API-driven resource creation
- persistent volumes
- useful telemetry
- acceptable resource overhead
- automation that doesn't become its own full-time job?

THEN
Add future hardware as OpenStack-capable compute
rather than dismantling working infrastructure first.
```

That avoids one of the classic homelab mistakes: destroying the working system so you can build the infrastructure that will eventually replace the working system.

And there's another possibility I think is worth putting on the table now: **OpenStack may not actually be the winner.**

If the real GMRI requirement is “open-source private cloud OS with API-controlled compute/storage/networking and meaningful isolation,” then we should compare OpenStack against things like **Apache CloudStack, OpenNebula, Harvester, and perhaps Proxmox's own API plus a thinner orchestration layer**.

Because now we're asking the right question:

> **What should the GMRI private cloud be?**

Not:

> “How do we fake AWS so Agent Office works?”

That's a substantially more important systems decision.

And given the organization's scope, I think it deserves an actual architecture comparison rather than picking OpenStack because it happens to be the first serious hammer we found.
